name: Kabi Lungchok
tagline: Where a Lepcha seer and a Tibetan prince swore blood brotherhood
meta_description: Kabi Lungchok, 17 km north of Gangtok: the 13th-century blood-brotherhood stones of Thekong Tek and Khye Bumsa, Phensang Monastery, jeeps and costs.
summary: Kabi Lungchok is a historic site 17 km north of Gangtok on the North Sikkim road, where the Lepcha chief Thekong Tek and the Tibetan prince Khye Bumsa swore blood brotherhood in the 13th century. Stone pillars and statues mark it. No permit for Indians; an easy half-day by shared jeep.

local_story.title: The stone erected by our blood
paras: Sikkim's migration narratives tell of Khye Bumsa, a 13th-century prince of the Minyak house in Kham, eastern Tibet, who settled in the Chumbi valley. After three childless years, he crossed the passes into Sikkim to seek the blessing of a Lepcha holy man, Thekong Tek, who lived in a bamboo hut among his people. With the seer's blessing, the story goes, Khye Bumsa had three sons, and Thekong Tek foretold that his descendants would rule the land.

Khye Bumsa returned to give thanks, and the two men sealed an alliance at Kabi with a solemn oath of blood brotherhood, invoking the mountain gods and Kanchenjunga as witness: Lepchas and Bhutias would be as one family. Animals were sacrificed, and stones were set up to mark the pact. The name is often explained as stone erected by our blood. In 1642 Phuntsog Namgyal, counted as Khye Bumsa's descendant, became the first Chogyal of Sikkim. Today life-size statues of the two blood brothers stand at the site.

did_you_know: Kabi Lungchok is 17 km north of Gangtok on the North Sikkim Highway, and it gives its name to one of Mangan district's three assembly constituencies.
Some accounts say the pact at Kabi brought together three peoples: the Lepchas (Mon), the Limbus (Tsong) and the Bhutias (Lho).
Kabi village had 1,590 people in 323 households at the 2011 census.
intro: Kabi Lungchok is a short stop with a long story. Just off the North Sikkim road, a path leads to a quiet site among trees where standing stones mark the place of the oath, with a memorial, prayer flags and statues of Thekong Tek and Khye Bumsa. It takes half an hour to see, and a lifetime for Sikkimese to explain.

Most North Sikkim tours drive past without stopping, which is a pity. If you are travelling independently, take a shared jeep from Gangtok, spend the morning at Kabi and nearby Phensang Monastery, and continue to Phodong or back to Gangtok. No permit is needed for Indian nationals. Foreign nationals on a North Sikkim permit can usually stop here too.
facts: Jio, Airtel and BSNL usually work
costs: Shared jeep seat from Gangtok (Vajra stand)
Tea and momos on the highway

highlights.title: The oath stones
highlights.text: Standing stones mark where Thekong Tek and Khye Bumsa swore blood brotherhood in the 13th century. Walk round slowly, read the boards and think about how much Sikkim's later history rests on this spot.

highlights.title: Statues of the blood brothers
highlights.text: Life-size figures of the Lepcha seer and the Tibetan prince stand at the site, a modern memorial to an old pact. A good place to explain the story to children.

highlights.title: Phensang Monastery
highlights.text: A Nyingma monastery on the same road, established in 1721 in the time of Jigme Pawo. Combine it with Kabi for a morning of early Sikkimese history.

highlights.title: An easy half-day from Gangtok
highlights.text: Only 17 km out, with shared jeeps from the Vajra stand. Ideal for an acclimatisation day before North Sikkim or a quiet morning away from MG Marg.

highlights.title: On the way north
highlights.text: If you are on a North Sikkim tour, ask the driver for 20 minutes here. Many agree if you ask in Gangtok before leaving.

how_to_reach.text: Take any shared jeep from Gangtok's Vajra stand heading for Mangan, Phodong or Kabi and ask to be dropped at Kabi Lungchok, about ₹80–150 and 45 minutes to an hour. To return, wave down a jeep heading to Gangtok; they are frequent until early afternoon.
A taxi from Gangtok to Kabi, Phensang and Phodong and back costs about ₹2,500–3,500 for a half to full day. Agree the stops and waiting time in advance.
Tours to Lachung and Lachen pass Kabi about an hour after leaving Gangtok. Ask your agent to include a 20-minute stop; it costs nothing extra.

where_to_stay: Most people visit Kabi as a half-day trip from Gangtok, which has rooms at every budget. If you want to stay north of the city, Phodong, about 20 km further, has a few small guesthouses and homestays, and Singhik and Mangan, about two hours on, have lodges and budget hotels. There are some homestays in the villages around Kabi; ask in Gangtok or locally, and check what is currently operating.
tips: Go in the morning, when shared jeeps are frequent in both directions.
Combine Kabi with Phensang Monastery and Phodong for a full day of early Sikkim history.
Treat the site as sacred: no climbing on the stones, no loud music.
Ask your North Sikkim tour driver in Gangtok, not on the road, for a stop here.
Carry small notes for jeep fares and tea.

experiences.title: The oath stones of Thekong Tek and Khye Bumsa
experiences.summary: Stand where Sikkim's Lepcha and Bhutia peoples are said to have become one family. The standing stones, memorial and statues at Kabi Lungchok mark the 13th-century oath between the Lepcha seer Thekong Tek and the Tibetan prince Khye Bumsa.
body: The path from the road leads into a quiet site among trees. In the centre stand the stones that mark the oath, with prayer flags and a memorial. Nearby are life-size statues of the two men: Thekong Tek, the Lepcha chief and holy man, and Khye Bumsa, the prince from Kham in eastern Tibet whose descendants became Sikkim's royal family.

The story, told in Sikkimese and Tibetan narratives, is that Khye Bumsa came to Thekong Tek for a blessing to have children, received it, and returned to give thanks. They swore blood brotherhood here, calling on the mountain gods and Kanchenjunga as witness. In 1642 Phuntsog Namgyal, counted as Khye Bumsa's descendant, was enthroned as the first Chogyal.

Walk round the site clockwise and read the boards. Do not climb on the stones or tie anything to them. The site is used for ceremonies, and Sikkimese of all communities treat it with respect. Children enjoy the statues; it is a good place to tell them the story.

faqs.q: What happened at Kabi Lungchok?
faqs.a: In the 13th century, according to Sikkimese and Tibetan narratives, the Lepcha chief and seer Thekong Tek and the Tibetan prince Khye Bumsa swore an oath of blood brotherhood at Kabi Lungchok. The pact bound Lepchas and Bhutias as one people. Stone pillars mark the site, and statues of the two men stand there today.

faqs.q: Who was Khye Bumsa?
faqs.a: Khye Bumsa is named in Sikkimese migration narratives as a 13th-century prince of the Minyak house from Kham in eastern Tibet, who settled in the Chumbi valley. Sikkim's Chogyals, beginning with Phuntsog Namgyal in 1642, traced their descent from him.

faqs.q: Is there an entry fee at Kabi Lungchok?
faqs.a: No, entry is free and the site is open in daylight. There is no ticket office or guide service. Read the information boards, and if you want deeper history, visit the Namgyal Institute of Tibetology in Gangtok before or after.

experiences.title: Phensang Monastery on the North Sikkim road
experiences.summary: Phensang is a Nyingma monastery on the slopes north of Gangtok, established in 1721 in the time of Jigme Pawo. Combine it with Kabi Lungchok for a morning of early Sikkimese history, and visit at prayer time if you can.
body: Phensang Monastery belongs to the Nyingma school, the oldest of Tibetan Buddhism's four schools and the one most associated with Sikkim. It was established in 1721, during the time of Jigme Pawo, regarded as a reincarnation of Lhatsun Chenpo, the lama credited with consecrating the first Chogyal in 1642.

The monastery sits on a slope off the North Sikkim road, with a courtyard, a prayer hall and monks' quarters. In the morning you may hear prayers and drums. Inside, look for images of Guru Padmasambhava and the protector deities. It is a working monastery, not a museum, so visiting hours are informal.

Shared jeeps heading north can drop you at the turn-off; ask the driver. Dress modestly, remove shoes before entering, walk clockwise, and ask before photographing inside. A small donation of ₹50–100 is welcome. The monastery holds annual rituals and masked dances; dates follow the Tibetan calendar, so ask locally.

faqs.q: When was Phensang Monastery founded?
faqs.a: Phensang Monastery was established in 1721, during the time of Jigme Pawo. It belongs to the Nyingma school of Tibetan Buddhism and lies on the slopes north of Gangtok, near the North Sikkim road between Gangtok and Kabi.

faqs.q: How do I reach Phensang Monastery?
faqs.a: Take a shared jeep from Gangtok's Vajra stand toward Kabi or Mangan and ask to be dropped at the Phensang turn-off, then walk up. A reserved taxi from Gangtok covering Phensang, Kabi Lungchok and Phodong costs about ₹2,500–3,500 for the day.

faqs.q: Is Phensang worth visiting if I have seen Rumtek?
faqs.a: Yes, for a different feel. Rumtek is a large Kagyu seat with many visitors. Phensang is a smaller Nyingma monastery with fewer tourists and a quieter atmosphere, and it fits naturally with Kabi Lungchok and Phodong into a half-day of early Sikkim history.

experiences.title: A morning walk through Kabi's farm villages
experiences.summary: Around Kabi, footpaths link small farms of maize, vegetables, cardamom and oranges on terraces above the North Sikkim road. Walk an easy loop for two hours after visiting the stones, see how families farm the slope, and catch a jeep onward or back.
body: Kabi is a farming village of about 1,600 people spread across the slopes around the historic site. Families grow maize, vegetables, ginger and cardamom, keep cows and goats, and in lower fields grow mandarin oranges. The paths between houses and fields are the village's own roads, and a slow walk shows you mid-hill Sikkim at its everyday best.

There is no marked trail. From the Kabi Lungchok site, follow paths up or down the slope for an hour, ask villagers the way back to the road, and keep to the edges of fields. Mornings are clearest; from October to April you may glimpse snow peaks to the north and west on clear days.

Be courteous: greet people, ask before photographing homes or people, and do not pick fruit. Dogs may bark but are usually tied. Wear shoes with grip; paths are steep and slippery after rain. When you are done, wave down a shared jeep on the main road toward Phodong or Gangtok.

faqs.q: Can I walk around Kabi village?
faqs.a: Yes. Footpaths link houses and fields around Kabi, and walkers are welcome if they are courteous and keep to paths. There is no marked route or guide service. Ask villagers for directions and stay on field edges. Mornings from October to May are best.

faqs.q: Are there homestays in Kabi?
faqs.a: Some families around Kabi run small homestays, but we cannot vouch for specific ones. Ask in Gangtok or locally and check reviews and current status. Many visitors make Kabi a half-day trip from Gangtok or continue to Phodong, Mangan or Singhik for the night.

faqs.q: What crops grow around Kabi?
faqs.a: Maize, vegetables, ginger, large cardamom in shaded patches and mandarin oranges in lower, warmer fields, along with fodder for cows and goats. Like all of Sikkim, Kabi's farming has been officially organic since 2016.

experiences.title: Sha phaley and tea on the North Sikkim road
experiences.image_query: Sha phaley Tibetan fried bread meat
experiences.summary: Roadside eateries along the North Sikkim road near Kabi and Phodong serve tea, momos, thukpa and sha phaley, the Tibetan-style bread stuffed with seasoned meat and fried or baked. It is a cheap, filling lunch between the stones and the monasteries.
body: Sha phaley is a Tibetan dish common in Sikkim: dough stuffed with seasoned minced meat, sometimes cabbage, sealed into a half-moon or round and shallow-fried until crisp. In small eateries along the highway north of Gangtok you find it alongside momos, thukpa, chowmein and sweet milk tea.

Expect ₹100–180 for a plate of sha phaley or a bowl of thukpa, ₹80–150 for momos and ₹15–30 for tea. Vegetarian versions with cabbage or potato are common. On a North Sikkim tour, drivers often stop at their favourite places; independent travellers can ask the jeep driver where locals eat.

Eat light if you are continuing north on a winding road; heavy fried food and hairpins do not mix. Carry water. Many eateries close by mid-afternoon, so do not leave lunch too late. Pay cash; small places rarely take cards, though UPI may work when the network is good.

faqs.q: What is sha phaley?
faqs.a: Sha phaley is a Tibetan dish of bread dough stuffed with seasoned meat and cabbage, shaped into half-moons or rounds and fried or baked until crisp. It is popular across Sikkim, especially in Gangtok and along the North Sikkim road, and costs about ₹100–180 a plate.

faqs.q: Where can I eat near Kabi Lungchok?
faqs.a: Small eateries along the North Sikkim road near Kabi and further on at Phodong serve tea, momos, thukpa and sha phaley. They are simple and cheap. For a wider choice, eat in Gangtok before setting out or in Mangan if you are continuing north.

faqs.q: Is food on the North Sikkim highway safe?
faqs.a: Generally yes, in busy places with high turnover where food is cooked fresh. Choose steaming momos and hot soups over items left sitting out, and drink bottled or filtered water. If you have a sensitive stomach, eat lightly before the winding drive.

faqs.q: How far is Kabi Lungchok from Gangtok?
faqs.a: Kabi Lungchok is about 17 km north of Gangtok on the North Sikkim Highway, roughly 45 minutes to an hour by road. Shared jeeps from the Vajra stand toward Mangan or Phodong pass it, and a seat costs about ₹80–150.

faqs.q: Why is Kabi Lungchok important?
faqs.a: It is where, according to Sikkimese and Tibetan narratives, the Lepcha chief Thekong Tek and the Tibetan prince Khye Bumsa swore blood brotherhood in the 13th century, uniting Lepchas and Bhutias. The Chogyal dynasty that ruled Sikkim from 1642 traced its descent from Khye Bumsa.

faqs.q: Do I need a permit for Kabi Lungchok?
faqs.a: Indian nationals do not need a permit for Kabi Lungchok. Foreign nationals need the Protected Area Permit for North Sikkim; Kabi is usually visited on the way north with that permit. Check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: How much time do I need at Kabi Lungchok?
faqs.a: About 30–45 minutes for the site itself. Add an hour for Phensang Monastery and two hours for a village walk. A half-day trip from Gangtok covers Kabi and Phensang; a full day adds Phodong and Labrang monasteries.

faqs.q: Can I visit Kabi Lungchok on a North Sikkim tour?
faqs.a: Yes, if you ask. Tours to Lachung and Lachen pass Kabi about an hour after leaving Gangtok. Ask your agent in Gangtok to include a 20-minute stop, and remind the driver when you set off. Most agree.

faqs.q: What does Kabi Lungchok mean?
faqs.a: The name is commonly explained as stone erected by our blood, referring to the stones set up to mark the blood-brotherhood oath. It is also spelled Kabi Longstok. The meaning is a popular interpretation; scholars may give other derivations.

faqs.q: Is Kabi Lungchok good for children?
faqs.a: Yes. It is short, safe and close to Gangtok, and the statues of the two blood brothers make the story easy to tell. Combine it with a stop at a roadside eatery and Phensang Monastery for an easy half-day.

faqs.q: What is the best time to visit Kabi Lungchok?
faqs.a: Any time from October to May, in the morning or early afternoon. The monsoon, June to September, brings rain and occasional landslides on the North Sikkim road but the site itself stays open. Check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: Is Kabi Lungchok connected to Pang Lhabsol?
faqs.a: Yes, in tradition. Pang Lhabsol, a Sikkimese festival in late summer that honours Kanchenjunga as guardian deity, is also linked to the memory of the blood-brotherhood oath. Its main masked dances are held in Gangtok and elsewhere, not at Kabi itself.
